overview.title: Intelligence + Continual Learning = Expertise
overview.speaker: Yu Su
overview.main_topic: The distinction between AI intelligence and AI expertise, and why continual learning is the bridge between them.
overview.executive_summary: Yu Su explores the conceptual distinction between raw AI intelligence and domain-specific expertise, arguing that while language agents have achieved remarkable general capabilities, they struggle in everyday digital work because they lack situated competence and continual learning. By framing continual learning as the adaptive compression of experience into reusable structures, he presents a vision for unbounded expertise from bounded intelligence.
overview.purpose: To provide conceptual clarity on why AI agents succeed at coding but struggle with broader enterprise and personal workflows, and to advocate for continual learning as the missing link for scalable AI expertise.

topic_map.explanation: Introduction of the speaker and the foundational thesis that intelligence and expertise are orthogonal concepts in AI.
key_claims: We are standing between intelligence and expertise.
Current agents are good at coding but terrible at everything else.
Current agents are token-inefficient.
examples: Company token-maxing efforts in enterprise settings.
topic_map.why_it_matters: Establishes the core problem facing AI engineering as we move beyond prompt engineering.

topic_map.topic: The Evolution of AI Agents and the Coding Mass Market
topic_map.explanation: A historical overview of AI agents moving from logical to neural to language agents, and why coding became their first mass market.
key_claims: Language agents represent a new evolutionary stage of machine intelligence.
Coding is the ideal mass market because code is already a language-native world.
Anthropic revenue grew 400x in under two years driven largely by coding capabilities.
examples: Anthropic annualized run rate growth graph.
topic_map.why_it_matters: Explains why coding succeeded while other domains failed due to symbolic grounding.

topic_map.explanation: Adapting Moravec's paradox to the digital world: symbolic reasoning is easy for AI, while everyday digital work is hard.
key_claims: Hard things are easy and easy things are hard for AI in the digital era.
Modern society is made of millions of micro-worlds with unique local physics.
Monolithic models cannot compress the heterogeneous and dynamic world into a single static representation.
examples: Iceberg diagram showing symbolic reasoning above water and everyday digital work below water.
topic_map.why_it_matters: Identifies why deploying AI agents in enterprise and personal settings leads to brittle failures.

topic_map.explanation: Working definitions establishing the fundamental differences between intelligence and expertise.
key_claims: Intelligence is the capacity to reason through unfamiliar problems from available context.
Expertise is accumulated and situated competence in a particular domain.
Experts don't just know more facts; they see the world differently.
topic_map.why_it_matters: Clarifies why scaling raw intelligence alone does not produce reliable domain experts.

topic_map.explanation: Defining continual learning as adaptive compression of experience into reusable structures for future behavior.
key_claims: Continual learning is the bridge from intelligence to expertise.
Continual learning is adaptive compression of experience into reusable structure.
Without continual learning, super-smart models remain novices that brute-force every problem.
examples: Mapping out what experience means, how it is compressed, what structures are formed, and how they are used.
topic_map.why_it_matters: Provides a rigorous framework for thinking about memory and learning in AI systems.

topic_map.topic: The Scaling of Expertise and Escape Intelligence
topic_map.explanation: Analyzing the orthogonal relationship between raw intelligence and expertise, introducing the concept of escape intelligence.
key_claims: Raw intelligence and expertise are largely orthogonal on a graph.
Continual learning sets the slope of the expertise curve.
Unbounded expertise from bounded intelligence (escape intelligence) occurs once raw intelligence crosses a threshold.
examples: Graphs plotting expertise versus raw intelligence with different continual learning slopes.
topic_map.why_it_matters: Suggests that after a certain intelligence threshold, better continual learning matters more than raw model scale.

topic_map.topic: Open Questions and Call to Action
topic_map.explanation: Listing open research questions and calling for a focus on scaling AI expertise.
key_claims: We need to answer how to measure expertise and handle the reliability-plasticity tradeoff.
Intelligence is becoming abundant, but expertise is still scarce.
Every company needs to build a learning loop turning human-AI interactions into institutional memory.
examples: Healthcare, finance, tutoring, and executive assistant use cases.
topic_map.why_it_matters: Outlines the future research agenda and economic impact of scaling AI expertise.

key_points.explanation: Intelligence is general and handles unfamiliar contexts via inference-time reasoning, whereas expertise is situated, accumulated, and compresses search.
key_points.evidence: Definitions and comparative breakdown between intelligence and expertise dimensions.
key_points.practical_implication: AI engineering must shift focus from building smarter base models to building continual learning mechanisms that cultivate domain expertise.

key_points.explanation: While AI excels at abstract symbolic tasks like math and coding, it struggles with messy everyday digital work across heterogeneous micro-worlds.
key_points.evidence: MIT reports on generative AI pilot failures and brittle prompt-based error examples.
key_points.practical_implication: Deploying agents outside sandboxed coding environments requires handling local physics, constraints, and affordances.

key_points.explanation: Continual learning compresses diverse experiences (episodes, facts, procedures, feedback) into reusable structures (parameters, vectors, graphs, skills, world models) used for future planning and control.
key_points.evidence: Four-element framework mapping experience, compression, structure, and usage.
key_points.practical_implication: Systems must continuously learn on the job rather than relying solely on static pre-training.

frameworks.name: The Four Dimensions of Continual Learning
frameworks.how_it_works: Breaks down continual learning into what experience is gathered, how it is compressed, what structure it forms, and how that structure is used.
components: Structure (parameters, vectors, graphs, skills, world models)
frameworks.when_to_use: When designing agent architectures that need to adapt and improve over time in complex domains.

examples.what_happened: Coding agents achieving massive commercial success (Anthropic run rate growth).
examples.illustrates: Why language agents found their first mass market in coding.
examples.lesson: Coding is language-native with symbolic goals, tools, errors, and rewards already structured.

immediate: Recognize the difference between intelligence (solving from context) and expertise (bringing the right context).
Understand that coding success does not automatically generalize to messy digital workflows.
strategic: Invest in continual learning architectures to convert raw intelligence into situated expertise.
Build human-AI learning loops inside enterprises to establish institutional memory.
questions_to_investigate: How to measure expertise in specific environments?
How to balance the trade-off between system reliability and plasticity?
How to synergize parametric and non-parametric learning?

claims_to_verify.claim: Anthropic annualized run rate grew to 40 billion or 60 billion in under two years.
MIT report states 95 percent of generative AI pilots at companies are failing.

quotes.text: Coding is the first mass market because code is already a language-native world.
Continual learning is adaptive compression of experience into reusable structure for future behavior.

bullets: Intelligence is general reasoning from context, while expertise is situated competence accumulated over time.
Modern Moravec's Paradox highlights that AI easily handles symbolic coding but struggles with heterogeneous micro-worlds in everyday digital work.
Continual learning is defined as the adaptive compression of experience into reusable structures for future behavior.
Effective continual learning sets the slope for turning bounded intelligence into unbounded expertise.
compressed.core_insight: Raw intelligence without continual learning leaves AI models as smart novices; continual learning is the essential bridge to domain expertise.
